sec.t:
कॉमनवेल्थ खाड़ी की हवा तूफ़ानों से नहीं आती। यह ख़ुद [[@antarctica|अंटार्कटिका]] की बनावट से आती है। महाद्वीप का बीच का हिस्सा बर्फ़ का एक विशाल गुंबद है, कहीं-कहीं 3 किलोमीटर से भी ज़्यादा मोटा। उसके ऊपर की हवा बेहद ठंडी हो जाती है, और ठंडी हवा भारी होती है।

वह भारी हवा तट की ओर ढलान से नीचे फिसलती है, जैसे छत से पानी बहता है। कॉमनवेल्थ खाड़ी पर ढलान और खड़ी हो जाती है, और हवा एक सँकरी धारा में सिमट जाती है। वह रफ़्तार पकड़ती है और समुद्र की ओर उमड़ पड़ती है। ऐसी हवाओं को कैटाबेटिक कहते हैं, जो एक यूनानी शब्द से है, जिसका मतलब है "नीचे जाती हुई"।

sec.h: एक पहाड़ जिसके नाम था रिकॉर्ड
sec.t:
60 से ज़्यादा सालों तक सबसे तेज़ झोंके का रिकॉर्ड अमेरिका के न्यू हैम्पशायर के माउंट वॉशिंगटन के नाम था। 12 अप्रैल 1934 को उसकी चोटी पर बने मौसम केंद्र के वैज्ञानिकों ने 372 किमी/घंटा (231 मील प्रति घंटा) का झोंका नापा। इस चोटी पर कई दिशाओं से तूफ़ान आते हैं, और यह ज़मीन से बहुत ऊपर चलने वाली तेज़ हवाओं के रास्ते में है।

2010 में आधिकारिक [[@weather-records|मौसम रिकॉर्डों]] के रखवाले विश्व मौसम विज्ञान संगठन ने 1996 की बैरो द्वीप वाली नाप की जाँच की और उसे नया विश्व रिकॉर्ड मान लिया। माउंट वॉशिंगटन अब भी उस रिकॉर्ड का दावा करता है कि लोगों वाले केंद्र पर नापा गया सबसे तेज़ झोंका उसी का है।

किसी ताकतवर बवंडर के अंदर हवा इन सबसे तेज़ हो सकती है, पर उसे नापना मुश्किल है। ज़मीन पर रखे उपकरण आम तौर पर तबाह हो जाते हैं। 1999 में ओक्लाहोमा सिटी के पास एक [[@tornadoes|बवंडर]] में एक रडार ट्रक ने लगभग 480 किमी/घंटा की हवाएँ नापीं। रडार ज़मीन से ऊपर की हवा नापता है, इसलिए वह आँकड़ा एक अलग सूची में रखा जाता है।

तेज़, लगातार चलती हवा क़ीमती भी है। तमिलनाडु में कन्याकुमारी के पास मुप्पंदल इलाके में हज़ारों [[turbine|टरबाइनें]] पश्चिमी घाट के एक दर्रे से बहती हवा को पकड़ती हैं। गुजरात, कर्नाटक और दूसरे राज्यों में भी बड़े पवन फ़ार्म हैं।

इंजीनियर ऐसी जगहें खोजते हैं जहाँ हवा तेज़ तो हो पर बेलगाम नहीं, क्योंकि कॉमनवेल्थ खाड़ी जैसे झोंके किसी मशीन को चीर डालेंगे। असल में [[@wind-turbines|पवन चक्की]] के लिए सबसे अच्छी जगह वह है जहाँ एक जैसी हल्की बयार चलती हो, उस हवा से कहीं नरम जिसने मॉसन के साथियों को बर्फ़ पर चिपका दिया था।

text: सोने के [[atom|परमाणु]] धरती पर नहीं बनते। सूरज जैसे आम तारे कार्बन और ऑक्सीजन जैसे हल्के [[element|तत्व]] बना सकते हैं, पर सोने जैसे भारी तत्व नहीं। उसके लिए कहीं ज़्यादा ज़बरदस्त कुछ चाहिए।

वैज्ञानिकों का मानना है कि ज़्यादातर सोना तब बना जब दो [[@space-weird-neutron-spoon|न्यूट्रॉन तारे]] आपस में टकराए। न्यूट्रॉन तारे मरे हुए तारों के बचे हुए, बेहद ठसे हुए टुकड़े होते हैं। इस टक्कर ने सोना और दूसरी भारी धातुएँ अंतरिक्ष में बिखेर दीं। उस धूल का कुछ हिस्सा उस बादल में पहुँचा जिससे हमारा सौरमंडल बना। बाद में धरती के अंदर गर्म पानी और खिसकती चट्टानों ने सोने को नसों जैसी धारियों में जमा कर दिया, जहाँ खनिक उसे ढूँढ लेते हैं।

sec.t:
अगस्त 2017 में अमेरिका और इटली के यंत्रों ने खुद अंतरिक्ष में उठी लहरें पकड़ीं, जिन्हें गुरुत्व तरंगें कहते हैं। ये लगभग 13 करोड़ [[@light-years|प्रकाश वर्ष]] दूर टकराते दो न्यूट्रॉन तारों से आई थीं। फिर दुनिया भर की [[telescope|दूरबीनें]], नासा के अंतरिक्ष यानों समेत, उस ओर मुड़ गईं। उन्हें ताज़ा बने भारी तत्वों की चमक दिखी।

माना गया कि उस एक टक्कर में इतना सोना बना जिसका वज़न धरती से कई गुना था। कुछ वैज्ञानिक सोचते हैं कि कुछ दुर्लभ फटते तारे, एक तरह के [[@supernova|सुपरनोवा]], भी सोना बनाते हैं। बहस इस पर है कि किस घटना का कितना हाथ है।

जनवरी 1848 में जेम्स मार्शल नाम के एक बढ़ई को कैलिफ़ोर्निया में सटर्स मिल के पास एक नाले में चमकते कण दिखे। साल भर के अंदर हज़ारों-हज़ार लोग पश्चिम की ओर चल पड़े। 1849 के साल के नाम पर उन्हें [[@gold-rush|"फ़ोर्टी-नाइनर्स"]] कहा गया। [[@san-francisco|सैन फ़्रांसिस्को]] का छोटा-सा बंदरगाह लगभग रातों-रात शहर बन गया।

भारत में भी सोने की खुदाई का लंबा इतिहास है। [[@karnataka|कर्नाटक]] में बेंगलुरु से लगभग 100 किमी दूर कोलार गोल्ड फ़ील्ड्स की सुरंगें 3 किमी से भी ज़्यादा गहरी थीं, दुनिया की सबसे गहरी खदानों में से। यह 2001 में बंद हो गई। कर्नाटक की हट्टी खदान से आज भी सोना निकलता है।

सोना उतने ही पानी से लगभग 19 गुना भारी होता है। तो पूरे इतिहास में खोदे गए करीब 2,00,000 टन सोने को 19 से भाग दो, तो वह सिर्फ़ लगभग 11,000 घन मीटर जगह भरता है। इससे लगभग 22 मीटर भुजा वाला घन बनता है, जो किसी सात मंज़िला इमारत जितना ऊँचा होगा।

इसके लिए खनिकों को बहुत मेहनत करनी पड़ती है। आज की एक आम खदान में एक टन चट्टान में शायद कुछ ही ग्राम सोना होता है, बस एक अँगूठी जितना।

text: Astronauts train for years before they fly. They learn how a spacecraft works, how to fix it and what to do if something goes wrong. They practise moving and working without weight, survive in the wild in case they land somewhere remote, and study science for the experiments they will run.
Most astronauts spend about two years in basic training. After they are picked for a particular mission, they train for another year or two with their crew.

Much of it is like school. There are classes, exams and endless practice. The rest is more like an adventure camp, with diving, flying, camping in snow and learning to work as a team when things go wrong.

sec.t:
Spacewalks are some of the hardest jobs in space. To practise them, NASA built the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston, Texas. It is a pool 12 m (40 feet) deep, holding about 23 million litres of water, enough to fill about nine Olympic swimming pools.

Inside sit full-size copies of parts of the [[@space-station|space station]]. Astronauts in real spacesuits are lowered in. Divers add small weights and floats until each astronaut neither sinks nor rises. This trick, called neutral [[buoyancy|buoyancy]], is the closest thing to weightlessness you can keep up for hours.

A practice session can last six hours. Astronauts often spend several hours in the pool for every hour they will spend on a real spacewalk.

Some training happens in the air. A special plane climbs steeply, then curves over the top of an arc and dives. For about 20 to 25 seconds at a time, everyone inside floats.

The plane repeats the arc again and again on one flight. Many passengers feel sick, which is why the plane has the nickname "vomit [[comet|comet]]". Astronauts use these seconds to practise eating, drinking and moving around without weight.

Astronauts also ride a centrifuge, a machine that spins them around fast to pile on the heavy feeling of a rocket launch. And they learn to fly jets, which teaches them to stay calm and make quick choices.

{{story:space-body}}

Capsules sometimes come down far from where they were meant to. So astronauts practise surviving in forests, deserts, snow and the sea.

They learn to climb out of a bobbing capsule into a life raft, build shelters and keep warm until rescuers arrive. Russian training includes winter camps in the forest. Crews practise these skills together, because getting along matters as much as any skill when you are stuck in a small space for months.

On the International Space Station, crews from many countries live together. NASA astronauts learn Russian, and Russian cosmonauts learn English. Many controls on the Russian Soyuz spacecraft are labelled in Russian, so astronauts riding it must read them quickly.

Crews also study every system of the spacecraft they will live in, from the toilet to the oxygen supply, until they know them by heart. Up there, there is no repair shop to call.

In 2024 India named four Indian Air Force pilots as astronaut-designates for its [[@gaganyaan|Gaganyaan]] programme: Prasanth Nair, Ajit Krishnan, Angad Pratap and Shubhanshu Shukla. In 2020 and 2021 they trained at the Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Centre near Moscow, where they practised survival in snow, water and desert.

Since then they have trained at ISRO's own facility in Bengaluru, and some trained in the USA. In 2025 Shukla put it all to use, joining the short list of [[@indian-astronauts|Indian astronauts]] with about 18 days aboard the International Space Station. The rest of the group continue training for India's first crewed Gaganyaan flight.

text: Your weight depends on where you are standing. Weight is the pull of [[gravity|gravity]] on your body, and different planets and moons pull with different strengths. On a small world with weak gravity, you would weigh much less. On a giant like Jupiter, you would weigh much more.

Your [[@weights-mass|mass]], the amount of stuff you are made of, stays the same everywhere. A child who weighs 40 kilograms on Earth would still be the same child on the Moon, but a scale there would read only about 6.6 kilograms. Strictly speaking, scientists measure weight in newtons, a unit of force, but bathroom scales show kilograms, so this article uses those.

sec.t:
Two things decide how hard a planet pulls on you at its surface. One is its mass: more mass means stronger gravity. The other is its size: the farther you are from the planet's centre, the weaker the pull.

That's why some results surprise people. Saturn has 95 times Earth's mass, but it is so wide that at its cloud tops you'd weigh only about 7% more than at home. Mars has about twice Mercury's mass, yet Mercury's heavy iron core gives it the same surface pull, about 38% of Earth's.

sec.h: A trip around the solar system
sec.t:
Here is what a 40 kg child would weigh, using surface gravity numbers from NASA. The giant planets have no solid ground, so their numbers are for the cloud tops.

- **Moon:** about 6.6 kg
- **Mercury and Mars:** about 15 kg
- **Venus:** about 36 kg
- **Uranus:** about 35 kg
- **Saturn:** about 43 kg
- **Neptune:** about 45 kg
- **Jupiter:** about 101 kg
- **Pluto:** about 2.5 kg

To work out your own weight, multiply your Earth weight by 0.17 for the Moon, 0.38 for Mars or 2.5 for [[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter]].

The extremes are even stranger. If you could somehow stand on the Sun's glowing surface, that 40 kg child would weigh more than a tonne, about as much as a small car. On a tiny [[asteroid|asteroid]] only a few hundred metres across, the pull is so weak that a hard jump could launch you off into space for good.

{{story:newton-life}}

Weaker gravity changes how you move. On the Moon, a jump that lifts you 30 centimetres on Earth would carry you about 1.8 metres high, and you'd float down slowly. [[@apollo-moon|Apollo]] astronauts found that walking normally felt awkward, so many of them bounced along like kangaroos.

Heavy spacesuits that would crush you on Earth felt light on the Moon. The Apollo suits with their backpacks weighed around 80 kilograms on Earth, but only about 13 on the Moon. On Jupiter, by contrast, even standing up would feel like carrying another person on your back.

Our bodies are built for Earth's pull. Bones and muscles stay strong because they work against gravity every day. Astronauts who spend months on the space station, where they float, lose bone and muscle unless they exercise for about two hours a day. Doctors study what happens to [[@space-body|astronauts' bones]] to plan longer trips.

Mars's gravity is about 38% of Earth's. Nobody yet knows whether that is enough to keep a human body healthy over years. Scientists planning future [[@mars-colonies|Mars bases]] are trying to find out.

In 1687, Isaac [[@newton-life|Newton]] published his law of gravity, which says every object pulls on every other, with a strength that depends on their masses and the distance between them. The same rule explains why an apple falls, why the Moon [[orbit|orbits]] Earth and why you'd weigh more on Jupiter. You can test it, in a small way, every time you step on a scale.

text: Bird eggs get their colours from just two [[pigment|pigments]]. One, called protoporphyrin, makes reddish-brown colours and speckles. The other, biliverdin, makes blue and green. A bird adds them in a part of its body called the shell [[gland|gland]], in the last hours before the egg is laid. Mixing different amounts, and dabbing them in spots or streaks, gives everything from snowy white to deep blue to speckled brown.

Why each bird has its own colours is a harder question. Hiding eggs from hungry animals is a big reason for many birds. Others may be protecting eggs from sunlight, signalling health, or helping parents recognise their own eggs.

sec.t:
An egg forms inside a female bird over about a day. The shell builds up around it, made of calcium carbonate, the same material as chalk. Near the end, the shell gland adds colour. Blue-green pigment often goes right through the shell. Brown spots are usually added at the very end, on the surface.

Some brown-speckled eggs show which way the egg was turning as the colour went on. The spots can be smeared into streaks, like paint on a spinning wheel.

The common cuckoo lays its eggs in other birds' nests and lets them raise its chicks. Different groups of cuckoos specialise in different host birds, and their eggs often match the host's eggs closely in colour and pattern. Host birds that spot an odd egg may throw it out, so a good match helps the cuckoo.

In India, the koel lays its eggs in crows' nests. Its eggs look quite like crows' eggs, which may help them escape notice.

The American robin's eggs are such a clean sky-blue that "robin's egg blue" became the name of a colour. Many thrushes and [[@sky-murmurations|starlings]], including India's common myna, lay blue eggs too.

Why blue? Scientists have several ideas. Blue-green pigment may help shield the growing chick from strong sunlight. Bright blue eggs may also show that the mother is healthy, because making the pigment uses up resources. The evidence is mixed, and the reason may differ from bird to bird.

For a long time, scientists thought coloured eggs were a bird invention. Then, in 2018, researchers tested [[fossil|fossil]] eggshells and found traces of both pigments in the eggs of some dinosaurs. Oviraptor, a feathered dinosaur, laid blue-green eggs.

That fits with what fossils show more and more clearly: [[@birds-dinosaurs|birds are living dinosaurs]]. Egg sizes vary wildly too. An ostrich egg is about 15 cm long and weighs about as much as two dozen hen's eggs, while some hummingbird eggs are no bigger than a pea. Whatever their colour, every one of them is built the same way, as you can read in [[@eggs|what is inside an egg]].

text: Parrots copy our words by listening carefully and then reshaping their own sounds until they match. They don't have vocal cords like ours. Instead, they make sounds with an organ called the [[syrinx|syrinx]], deep in the chest where the windpipe splits in two.

A parrot then shapes those sounds with its thick, muscly tongue, its throat and its beak, in a similar way to how we use our mouth. Their brains are especially good at learning new sounds, so a [[@pets-care|pet parrot]] that hears a word again and again may start to say it back.

sec.t:
Only a few groups of animals can learn brand-new sounds by copying them. Humans can, and so can parrots, songbirds and [[@hummingbirds|hummingbirds]]. Some whales, dolphins, bats and elephants can too.

Parrots are among the best of all. In 2015, scientists comparing bird brains found that parrots have the usual song-learning areas found in songbirds, plus an extra outer "shell" around them. This shell may be one reason parrots are such good copycats, able to mimic human speech, door bells and even ringing phones.

The tongue matters too. A parrot's tongue is thick and moves a lot, like ours. Scientists using X-ray videos have watched parrots move their tongues to change their sounds, much as we shape vowels.

This is where scientists disagree. Most talking parrots are copying sounds without knowing what the words mean.

But some seem to understand more. In 1977, the American scientist Irene Pepperberg began working with an African grey parrot named Alex. Over 30 years, Alex learned to name around 50 objects, seven colours and several shapes. He could answer questions like "What colour is the key?" or "How many blocks?", even about objects he had never seen before. Some scientists think Alex really understood. Others say he may have learned clever tricks without understanding in the way we do.

Guinness [[@world-records|World Records]] once listed a budgie named Puck as knowing more than 1,700 words. Budgies are small parrots, and some of them become chatterboxes.

The African grey is often called the best talker, but many kinds of parrots can learn words. Some songbirds copy sounds too. The Australian lyrebird can imitate camera shutters and chainsaws.

sec.h: Parrots in India and the USA
sec.t:
The green rose-ringed parakeet, the *tota*, is one of India's most familiar birds. Many people once kept them in cages, but catching and selling India's native parrots is now against the law. They belong in the wild, where they can talk to their flocks.

In San Francisco, a wild flock of parrots, mostly descended from escaped pets, has lived on Telegraph Hill for decades. The birds became famous after a film was made about them, and they are now part of the story of [[@san-francisco|San Francisco]]. For another brainy bird, read about [[@crow-smart|crows]]. And to see how differently we make sounds, read about your own [[@voice|voice]].

text: The loudest animal ever measured is the sperm whale. Its clicks can reach about 230 [[decibel|decibels]] underwater, among the loudest sounds made by any living thing. Sperm whales use them like sonar to find squid in the dark deep sea.

On land and in the air, the champions include the white bellbird of the Amazon, howler monkeys, lions and some cicadas. And the smallest show-offs are wild too. A snapping shrimp makes a bang that boils water. A water bug the size of a rice grain sings louder than a busy road.

sec.t:
Sound is measured in decibels, or dB. The scale jumps fast. Every extra 10 dB means about ten times more sound energy. A quiet library is about 30 dB, normal talking about 60 dB, and a loud rock concert about 110 dB. Sounds above about 120 dB can hurt your ears.

There's a catch. Underwater decibels use a different starting point from those in air, so a sound of 230 dB in the sea isn't the same as 230 dB in a room. Scientists subtract roughly 60 dB to compare them. Even so, a sperm whale's click is extraordinarily powerful.

sec.h: The shrimp with a sonic gun
sec.t:
Pistol shrimps, also called snapping shrimps, are only a few centimetres long. One claw is much bigger than the other. When it snaps shut, it shoots out a jet of water so fast that it forms a tiny bubble.

When the bubble collapses, it makes a crack of about 200 dB underwater and, for a split second, heats up to about 4,700°C, close to the temperature of the Sun's surface. The shock can stun small fish. Colonies of these shrimps are so noisy that submarines in the Second World War used their crackle to hide.

In 2019, scientists recording birds in the Brazilian Amazon measured the song of the male white bellbird at about 125 dB. That's louder than a chainsaw close up. The male sings his loudest note right at a female perched beside him.

Nobody is sure how she avoids hurting her ears. The bird is only about the size of a pigeon, yet its thick belly muscles squeeze out a note as loud as a pneumatic drill.

Howler monkeys of Central and South America have a special hollow bone in the throat that makes their calls boom. A group's dawn chorus can be heard about 5 km away through the forest.

A lion's roar reaches about 114 dB close up and can carry up to 8 km on a still night. In India, the lions of Gir roar to tell other prides where their [[territory|territory]] ends.

Some cicadas reach over 100 dB, loud enough to drown out conversation in a forest. And the water boatman *Micronecta scholtzi*, a bug about 2 mm long, sings at about 99 dB by rubbing a tiny part of its body against its belly. Luckily for us, most of its sound stays underwater.

Loud sounds help animals find mates, warn rivals, hunt in the dark or stay in touch across long distances. In thick forests or the deep sea, where you can't see far, sound is the best way to reach someone.

But some of the most important animal sounds are ones we can't hear at all. Elephants rumble so low that the sound travels through the ground for kilometres, and other elephants may pick it up through their feet, as you'll find in [[@elephants-talk|how elephants talk]].

text: Yes. A simple telescope needs only two lenses and a tube to hold them in line.

At the front goes a large, gently curved lens with a long focal length, the distance at which it brings light to a point. It collects light from something far away and makes a small, upside-down picture of it inside the tube. At the back goes a small, strongly curved lens, the eyepiece. You look through it like a [[@magnifying-glass|magnifying glass]], enlarging that little picture.
To work out how much the telescope magnifies, divide the focal length of the front lens by that of the eyepiece. A front lens of 50 cm and an eyepiece of 5 cm gives ten times.

sec.t:
Many children's science kits and astronomy clubs offer simple telescope kits with cardboard tubes and two lenses. In 2009, the International Year of Astronomy, scientists designed a cheap kit called the Galileoscope so students around the world could build one and see Jupiter's moons for themselves.

You can also try with lenses you have at home. A pair of weak reading glasses can serve as the front lens, and a strong magnifying glass as the eyepiece. Hold them in line and move them apart until a distant object comes into focus. You'll notice the view is upside down. That's normal for this design, and it doesn't matter for looking at the Moon.

Many people think a telescope's power is all about magnification. [[astronomer|Astronomers]] care more about its width, called the aperture. A wider lens or mirror collects more light, like a bigger bucket in the rain. More light means you can see fainter stars and finer detail.

Magnify too much with a small lens, and the picture just gets bigger, dimmer and blurrier. That's why serious astronomers build huge mirrors. In 1668, Isaac Newton made a telescope using a curved mirror instead of a front lens. Mirrors can be made much bigger than lenses without sagging or bending colours.

In the 1920s, an American engineer named Russell Porter helped start a club in Vermont where amateurs ground their own telescope mirrors by hand. The meeting, called Stellafane, still happens every summer, and amateur telescope making spread across the USA.

In India, the Indian Institute of Astrophysics runs the Vainu Bappu Observatory at Kavalur in Tamil Nadu. Its main telescope, named after the astronomer M. K. Vainu Bappu, has a mirror about 2.3 metres wide. Many Indian cities also have astronomy clubs and [[@planetariums|planetariums]] that hold star parties, where people bring telescopes to share. A home-made two-lens telescope won't show [[galaxy|galaxies]], but it will show the Moon's [[crater|craters]], which is where Galileo started too.

text: Saalumarada Thimmakka was a farm labourer from Karnataka who became one of India's best-loved tree planters. With her husband, Chikkaiah, she planted banyan saplings along the road between the villages of Hulikal and Kudur, near Bengaluru. Today 385 of those trees line about 4.5 km of highway, a green tunnel of shade over the traffic.

She never went to school and earned a few rupees a day working in a stone quarry. The name people gave her, Saalumarada, means "row of trees" in Kannada. She died in November 2025 at an age she gave as 114, honoured with a state funeral.

st.prompt: Thimmakka's banyan saplings grew beside a dusty road with no water supply. What did she do to keep them alive?

options.t: Carried water to them in pots and guarded them from cattle with thorny fences
Dug a canal from a nearby river
Waited for the monsoon and left them alone

st.reveal: For years she and her husband carried water by hand and wrapped young plants in thorny bushes so goats and cattle could not eat them. A sapling needs this care until its roots go deep.

d.try: With an adult, pick a young tree near your home or school. Tie a piece of string around its trunk at your knee height and mark the length. Check it once a month, and water the tree in dry weeks. After a year, compare the strings.
myth: Once you plant a tree, it looks after itself.
Young trees need water and protection for their first few years, and many planted saplings die without it. Thimmakka's trees survived because she looked after them every day.

sec.t:
Thimmakka married Chikkaiah when she was young. Years passed and they had no children, which in their village brought sadness and unkind talk. So the couple decided to raise trees instead.

They chose the [[@banyan|banyan]], India's national tree, partly because cuttings from it root easily. A banyan sends down roots from its branches, and these roots thicken into new trunks. The Great Banyan in Kolkata's botanical garden is about 250 years old and covers an area larger than two football fields. One tree can look like a whole grove.

The road had no water supply. The couple filled pots and carried them along the highway, walking kilometres each day after work. They planted new saplings in the [[monsoon|monsoon]], when rain did some of the work, and guarded them through the dry months.

Accounts of her life say they began small, with about ten saplings in the first year, and added more each year after that. The row grew a little longer every monsoon. Banyans grow fast once their roots are settled, but the first few summers are fragile, and a single dry month can kill a sapling.

Hungry goats and cattle were the biggest danger. The couple wrapped each young plant in thorny bushes to keep animals away. Year by year, the saplings grew taller than the people who watered them. Chikkaiah died in 1991, and Thimmakka carried on.

{{story:what-if-no-trees}}

sec.h: Why one row of trees matters
sec.t:
A big banyan can lower the ground temperature beneath it by several degrees on a hot afternoon. Its leaves pull [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] from the air through [[@photosynthesis|photosynthesis]], and its figs feed birds, bats and monkeys. A single old banyan can be home to dozens of kinds of animals.

Roads in India are often widened, and trees are the first things cut down. In 2019, a road plan threatened Thimmakka's banyans. She appealed, and the state government said it would look at other options. The trees still stood.

Thimmakka was invited to Delhi in 2019 to receive the Padma Shri, one of India's highest civilian honours. Photos from that day show her giving the President a blessing, a touch on the forehead, which made people smile across the country. In 2016 the BBC named her one of its 100 most influential women.

Her fame reached far beyond India. An environmental education group in California is named after her. She went on planting trees and visiting schools well into old age, often in a simple green sari.

Thimmakka was not alone. In Assam, [[@india-forest-man|Jadav Payeng]] planted a forest on a sandbar in the Brahmaputra. In Kenya, [[@wangari-maathai|Wangari Maathai]] started a movement in 1977 that has planted tens of millions of trees, and won a Nobel Peace Prize for it. None of them began with money or power. They began with one plant and a pot of water, and the strangest part is how long those small acts last: a banyan can keep growing for hundreds of years.

text: A newsroom is the office where journalists gather, check and write the news. For a morning newspaper, the work starts around midday and runs late into the night. Reporters go out to find stories. Editors decide which ones matter most and fix the writing. Photographers, page designers and fact-checkers all play their part.

The day is shaped by one thing: the deadline. When the clock runs out, the pages must go to the printing presses, whether or not every story is perfect. Then trucks, vans and bicycles carry the paper to homes before breakfast. Online news never stops, so many newsrooms now run all day and night.

st.prompt: In a news report, where do journalists usually put the most important facts?

options.t: In the very first sentence or two
Saved for the end, like a mystery
Spread evenly through the story

st.reveal: News reports often use the "inverted pyramid". The biggest facts come first, then details, then background. A busy reader who stops after one paragraph still knows what happened, and an editor short of space can cut from the bottom.

myth: Journalists put their own opinions into every news story.

Newspapers separate news reports from opinion. A news report tries to tell what happened, with facts and quotes. Opinion columns and editorials, usually on a separate page, are where writers argue a view.

sec.t:
A reporter's day often starts on the phone. They check with police stations, hospitals, courts and government offices, and follow up on tips from readers. Some reporters have a "beat", a subject they cover every day, such as sport, schools, science or the city council.

Then they go out. A reporter covering a flood might talk to families, officials and engineers, and take careful notes of exactly what each person said. Most try to answer six questions: who, what, when, where, why and how. A good quote is gold, but it must be the real words the person used.

By late afternoon, reporters are back at their desks, writing. Most news reports follow the inverted pyramid: the key facts in the first sentence, details after, background at the end. That way an editor can trim from the bottom without losing what matters.

Sub-editors, called copy editors in the USA, then check every name, number and spelling. They also write headlines that fit a tight space. Checking matters more than ever, because [[@fake-news|fake news]] spreads fast and one wrong fact can damage trust in a whole paper. If a reporter can't confirm something with a second source, it often stays out.

Late in the evening, the finished pages go to the press. The basic idea is the same as Gutenberg's [[@printing-press|printing press]], though today's machines run on huge rolls of paper and print tens of thousands of copies an hour. Bundles are stacked, tied and driven across the city through the night.

Online, the deadline never really arrives. A story goes up on the website within minutes, then gets updated as new facts come in. Many newsrooms now have a night team whose whole job is to watch for breaking news while everyone else sleeps, and a morning team that takes over at dawn.

sec.h: A reporter who raced the world
sec.t:
Some journalists make the news themselves. In 1889, Nellie Bly, a reporter for the New York World, set out to beat the record of Phileas Fogg, the hero of [[@jules-verne|Jules Verne's]] novel *Around the World in Eighty Days*. Travelling mostly by steamship and train, she sent reports home along the way. She arrived back in 72 days, and crowds met her at the station.

Today, a reporter might send a story from a phone in a village with one bar of signal. The rule is still the one Bly followed: get there, see it yourself, and tell readers what you found.

text: Malala Yousafzai is a Pakistani campaigner for girls' education. She grew up in the Swat Valley, where an armed group called the Taliban tried to stop girls going to school. As a child she spoke out against it, on the radio, on television and in a diary for the BBC.
In 2012, when she was 15, a gunman from the group attacked her on her school bus. She was badly hurt but survived after treatment in Pakistan and England.
Instead of going quiet, she spoke louder. In 2014, aged 17, she became the youngest person ever to win the [[@nobel-peace|Nobel Peace Prize]].

st.prompt: In 2009, when she was 11, what first made people notice Malala?

options.t: She wrote an online diary for the BBC under a secret name
She won a national cricket match
She became the youngest teacher in Pakistan

st.reveal: The BBC's Urdu service asked for a schoolgirl to describe life in Swat as armed groups tried to shut girls' schools. Malala wrote as "Gul Makai", which means cornflower. Her short entries were read across Pakistan.

Yousafzai M. with Lamb C. (2013) I Am Malala. Weidenfeld & Nicolson.

d.try: Keep a one-week school diary like Malala's. Each day, write three lines about something you learned and how it felt. At the end of the week, read it back and pick the one thing you would most hate to lose if school stopped tomorrow.
myth: Malala only became known after she was attacked.

She was already speaking out in Pakistan for years before. She wrote her BBC diary in 2009, appeared in a documentary, and won Pakistan's first National Youth Peace Prize in 2011, a year before the attack.

sec.t:
Swat is a green valley of rivers and mountains in northern Pakistan, once popular with holidaymakers. Malala's father, Ziauddin Yousafzai, ran a school there and believed girls should learn as much as boys.

From about 2007, the Taliban took control of parts of Swat. They destroyed many schools and ordered girls to stay home. Malala, who loved school and came top of her class, refused to accept it. She was [[@names-world|named after Malalai]], a brave young woman in Pashtun folk stories who rallied fighters in a battle in Afghanistan in 1880.

Even before the diary, Malala and her father spoke at press clubs and on local radio about the school closures. In 2009, an American journalist made a short documentary about the family for *The New York Times*, filming Malala on what was meant to be her last day of school.

That year, Pakistan's army fought to push the Taliban out of Swat. Malala's family, like hundreds of thousands of others, had to leave home for several months. When they returned, schools slowly reopened.

In 2011 she won Pakistan's first National Youth Peace Prize. The government named a school after her. She was becoming well known, which also made her a target.

On 9 October 2012, a gunman stopped Malala's school bus and shot her. Doctors in Pakistan saved her life, and she was flown to a hospital in Birmingham, England, to recover. Her family settled there.

On her 16th birthday in 2013, she spoke at the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] in New York. "One child, one teacher, one book and one pen can change the world," she said. The UN called the day Malala Day.

In 2014, Malala shared the Nobel Peace Prize with [[@kailash-satyarthi|Kailash Satyarthi]], an Indian campaigner against [[@child-labour|child labour]]. With her father, she started the Malala Fund, which pays for education projects for girls in many countries. In 2020, she graduated from the University of Oxford.

People in Pakistan have mixed feelings about her. Many see her as a hero. Others are suspicious of how much attention she gets from Western countries. Around the world, about 12 crore girls are still out of school, so her work is far from done.

text: Some Hindi films are so well known that their lines, songs and characters turn up in everyday talk, even among people who have never watched them. They include Mother India (1957), Mughal-e-Azam (1960), Sholay (1975), Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge (1995) and Lagaan (2001). Many families add their own favourites, from Guide and Anand to Mr India and 3 Idiots.

These films are classics for different reasons. Some broke records. Some won awards abroad. Others had songs that every wedding band still plays. Together, they tell the story of how Hindi cinema, often called [[@bollywood|Bollywood]], grew up.

st.prompt: Sholay's dusty village of Ramgarh looks like it's somewhere in north India. Where was it really built?

options.t: In the rocky hills of Ramanagara, Karnataka
In the Thar Desert, Rajasthan
Inside a film studio in Mumbai

st.reveal: The filmmakers built a whole village set among the granite hills near Bengaluru, and shot there for many months. Locals still call one of the hills "Sholay hills".

d.try: Hold a family song quiz. Each person picks one song from an old Hindi film and plays or hums the first few lines. Everyone else has to guess the film, the hero or the decade. Grandparents usually win, which is half the fun.
myth: Bollywood is the name for all Indian films.

Bollywood means the Hindi film industry based in Mumbai. India also makes huge numbers of films in Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada, Bengali, Marathi and other languages, and several of these industries are as big as Bollywood or bigger.
facts: First Indian film nominated for an Oscar
Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge at Maratha Mandir, Mumbai

sec.t:
India's first feature film, Raja Harishchandra, was made by [[@dadasaheb-phalke|Dadasaheb Phalke]] in 1913. It was silent. The first Indian talkie, Alam Ara, came in 1931, and from then on songs became part of almost every Hindi film.

In the 1950s, a golden age began. [[@raj-kapoor|Raj Kapoor]]'s Awaara (1951) was a huge hit in India and also in the Soviet Union, where people sang its songs in Russian. Guru Dutt's Pyaasa (1957) told the story of a struggling poet. Mother India (1957), directed by Mehboob Khan, showed a village woman raising her sons through hardship. It became the first Indian film nominated for an Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film.

Sholay (1975), directed by Ramesh Sippy, is an action film about two small-time crooks hired to catch a bandit, Gabbar Singh. It starred Dharmendra, [[@amitabh-bachchan|Amitabh Bachchan]], Hema Malini, Jaya Bhaduri and Sanjeev Kumar.

It started slowly at the box office, then grew by word of mouth. It ran for five years at Mumbai's Minerva cinema. Lines such as Gabbar's "Kitne aadmi the?" (How many men were there?) are still quoted everywhere. Ramgarh, the film's village, was built among the [[granite|granite]] hills of Ramanagara in Karnataka.

Better known as DDLJ, this 1995 romance starring Shah Rukh Khan and Kajol follows two young Indians who meet on a trip across Europe. It mixed foreign locations with family values, and audiences in India and abroad loved it.

DDLJ opened at Maratha Mandir, a cinema in [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], in October 1995. It has played there ever since, usually in a morning show. In October 2025 it completed 30 years, the longest run of any film in an Indian cinema.

In Lagaan (2001), villagers in British India play a [[@cricket-history|cricket]] match against their rulers to escape a heavy tax. The film was nominated for an Oscar. It is nearly four hours long, but many children remember it as the first long film they watched to the end.

Later classics include Taare Zameen Par (2007), about a boy with dyslexia, and 3 Idiots (2009), a comedy about the pressure on engineering students.

Many classics are remembered for their music as much as their stories. Singers such as [[@lata-mangeshkar|Lata Mangeshkar]], Mohammed Rafi and Kishore Kumar recorded songs that people still sing at parties and weddings. A film can fade, but a good song from it can live for generations.

India makes more feature films each year than any other country, in many languages. Only a few become classics. Those are the ones that grandparents, parents and children can all watch together and still argue about.

text: Long before cinema, people made pictures seem to move with spinning toys. A drum with slits, called a zoetrope, showed a running horse when you spun it and peered through. These toys worked because your eyes and brain blend quick pictures into one smooth movement, as [[@movies-move|moving pictures]] explains. Today's studios still rely on the same trick, as [[@animation-studios|modern animation]] shows.

The first animated films came in the early 1900s. In 1906, J. Stuart Blackton in the USA filmed a chalk drawing being changed bit by bit. In 1908, the French artist Émile Cohl made *Fantasmagorie*, a film of stick figures lasting under two minutes, that is often called the first fully animated cartoon.

st.prompt: In 1914, Winsor McCay made a film of a dinosaur named Gertie. How did he make her move?

options.t: He drew thousands of separate pictures by hand
He moved a clay model a little at a time
He filmed a lizard and painted over it

st.reveal: McCay and an assistant made thousands of drawings on rice paper. McCay drew Gertie on every sheet, while the assistant traced the background again and again, which is why it wobbles a little.

src: Britannica, Animation.
Library of Congress, Origins of American Animation, 1900–1921.
n.certNote: Historians disagree on which film counts as the first cartoon, because it depends on whether you count painted strips, chalk drawings or only films drawn frame by frame.

myth: Mickey Mouse was the first cartoon star.

Felix the Cat was a worldwide star almost ten years earlier, from 1919, and Gertie the Dinosaur was drawing crowds in 1914. Mickey became famous in 1928 because Steamboat Willie was one of the first cartoons with well-matched sound.

sec.t:
In 1892, the Frenchman Émile Reynaud opened a show in Paris called the Théâtre Optique. He painted pictures on long strips of see-through material and wound them past a lamp, projecting little stories onto a screen with music.

Reynaud's shows ran for years and drew around half a million people. But he worked the strips by hand, and they could not be copied easily. When film cameras arrived, his invention lost out. In despair, he later threw most of his strips into the River Seine.

Drawing every frame on paper was slow, so studios found shortcuts. Artists began drawing characters on clear sheets of plastic called cels, which could be laid over one painted background. This let a studio produce a short cartoon every couple of weeks.

Felix the Cat, a clever black cat drawn much like a [[@comics-art|comic strip]] hero, became the first cartoon star known around the world, from 1919. In 1928, Walt Disney's studio released *Steamboat Willie*, starring Mickey Mouse, with sound carefully matched to the action. Audiences loved hearing a cartoon whistle, and silent cartoons quickly faded away.

People once thought no one would sit through a long cartoon. Yet the German artist Lotte Reiniger spent about three years cutting paper silhouettes for *The Adventures of Prince Achmed* (1926), based on stories from the *[[@arabian-nights|Arabian Nights]]*. It is the oldest animated feature film that still survives.

In 1937 Disney released *Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs*, the first full-length cel-animated feature in colour and sound. Many in [[@hollywood|Hollywood]] had called it "Disney's folly". It became one of the biggest hits of its time.

Before films, "cartoon" meant a full-size sketch that artists drew to plan a painting or a woven wall hanging. In 1843, the British humour magazine *Punch* printed joke drawings it called "cartoons", poking fun at a contest for paintings in Parliament. The name stuck to funny drawings, and later to animated films too.

India has its own long line of cartoonists, from newspaper artists such as [[@famous-cartoonists|R. K. Laxman]] to the animators of today. Many of them began, like Cohl and McCay, with a pencil, a stack of paper and a lot of patience.

text: Makar Sankranti marks the moment the Sun appears to move into the sign of Makara, or Capricorn, in the Indian [[zodiac|zodiac]]. From now on, the days in India grow longer and the cold begins to ease. Farmers bring in their winter crops, and families celebrate with sesame sweets, bonfires and, in many places, kites.

Nobody can say for certain why kites became part of the day. Some say it gets people outdoors into the healthy winter sun. Others link it to the Sun's "climb" in the sky. Mostly, it is a tradition that grew because it is joyful, and once a whole city does it together, it sticks.

st.prompt: Most Indian festivals change date every year. Makar Sankranti nearly always falls on 14 or 15 January. Why?

options.t: It follows the Sun, not the Moon
The government fixed the date in 1950
It is always held on a full moon

st.reveal: Diwali and Holi follow the Moon, so they move around. Sankranti marks the day the Sun appears to enter the sign of Makara, so it stays close to the same date on the ordinary calendar.

d.try: Make a mini kite from a sheet of newspaper, two thin sticks from a broom and some cotton thread. Tie a long tail of paper strips to the bottom. Try flying it with and without the tail and notice which one wobbles less.
myth: Sharper glass-coated string is just part of the game and harmless to everyone else.
Glass-coated and nylon manja cut thousands of birds every year and have injured people riding scooters. Because nylon does not snap easily, the National Green Tribunal banned it across India in 2017.
facts: the Sun entering Makara (Capricorn) in the Indian zodiac

sec.t:
The same day is celebrated across India under different names. In Gujarat it is Uttarayan, from the Sanskrit for the Sun's northward journey. Tamil Nadu celebrates [[@onam-pongal|Pongal]] by boiling new rice until it overflows. Punjab lights Lohri bonfires the night before, and Assam feasts during [[@art-bihu|Magh Bihu]].

Because Sankranti follows the Sun, it lands on 14 or 15 January almost every year. Festivals that follow the Moon, such as Holi or Diwali, wander around by several weeks.

An [[@pop-kites-patang|Indian fighter kite]], or *patang*, is a diamond of thin paper on two [[@bamboo|bamboo]] sticks, with no tail. That makes it unstable, which sounds bad but is the point. A skilled flyer can make it dart and dive with tiny tugs of the string. Letting the string out quickly makes the kite swoop; pulling it in makes it climb. In a fight, the trick is to slide your string across your rival's at speed, so it saws through.

The string near the kite, called manja, was traditionally coated with rice paste and powdered glass to make it sharp. To learn how any kite stays up at all, see [[@kite-flying|how kites fly]].

Sharp manja cuts more than other strings. Every January, animal hospitals in Gujarat and Rajasthan treat thousands of injured pigeons, kites (the birds) and even [[@vultures-india|vultures]]. Riders on two-wheelers have also been badly hurt by strings stretched across roads.

Cheap nylon string, often called "Chinese manja", is worse because it barely breaks. In 2017, the National Green Tribunal banned nylon and synthetic manja across India. Many cities now run bird rescue camps during the festival, and plain cotton string is making a comeback.

About 1,700 years ago, Makar Sankranti fell close to the winter [[solstice|solstice]], the shortest day of the year. The Earth's spin [[axis|axis]] wobbles very slowly, like a spinning top, and this has shifted the stars against the seasons. Today the solstice comes around 21 December, while Sankranti stays in mid-January. The longer days that kite flyers celebrate had actually started three weeks earlier.

text: A podcast is a series of audio shows, a bit like radio programmes, that you can play whenever you want. Each show is called an episode. You can listen on a phone, a computer or a smart speaker, and you can pause, skip back or listen at double speed.

Podcasts cover almost everything: science, history, cricket, mysteries, cooking, stories for bedtime and interviews with interesting people. Anyone can make one. That freedom is the big difference from traditional [[@radio-shows|radio]], where a station decides what goes on air and when.

st.prompt: The word "podcast" comes from "broadcast" and the name of which device?

A pea pod, because episodes come in a row
A walkie-talkie called the Pod

st.reveal: The iPod, a music player made by Apple from 2001, was hugely popular when the word appeared in 2004. Today you can listen to podcasts on almost any phone, computer or smart speaker.

d.try: Record a five-minute podcast with a friend or family member on a phone. Pick one topic, such as your favourite animal, and plan three questions to ask each other. Record in a small room with cushions or curtains, which soak up echoes and make voices sound clearer.
myth: You need a professional studio to make a podcast.
Many popular podcasts started with a cheap microphone or just a phone in a quiet room. Clear planning and a good topic matter more than expensive equipment.
facts: a phone or computer and a microphone

sec.t:
In February 2004, the British journalist Ben Hammersley wrote an article in *The Guardian* about people putting radio-style shows online. Looking for a name, he suggested a few, including "podcasting", from iPod and broadcasting. The iPod was Apple's portable music player, the must-have gadget of that time.

The word caught on fast. In 2005, Apple added podcasts to its iTunes store, and the *New Oxford American Dictionary* named "podcast" its word of the year.

Long before podcasts, families gathered around radios for serials, comedies and mystery plays. Many podcasts bring back those old forms: a story told in parts, ending each time on a cliffhanger, a moment that makes you desperate to hear what happens next.

In 2014, an American podcast called *Serial*, which re-examined a real crime case over many episodes, became a huge hit and made millions of new people try podcasts. Since then, [[@newspapers|newspapers]], radio stations and schools have all started their own. India now has thousands of podcasts in [[@hindi-language|Hindi]], Tamil, Bengali, Marathi and other languages, from [[mythology|mythology]] retold for children to long interviews about cricket.

Listening leaves your eyes and hands free. People hear podcasts while travelling on a crowded local train, walking to school, cooking or doing [[@life-chores-world|chores]]. A voice in your ears can feel personal, as if the host is talking just to you.

Stories told aloud are also very old. Long before printing, India had storytellers who travelled from village to village, performing epics and folk tales. A good podcast host uses some of the same tricks: a pause before a surprise, a change of voice, a question left hanging.

Many podcasts are recorded with nothing more than a phone. The most important things are a quiet room, a clear plan and speaking close to the microphone. Soft things such as cushions, curtains and blankets help stop echoes.

Afterwards, free editing apps let you cut out mistakes and add music. Children's podcasts made by children themselves are now played in classrooms in India, the USA and many other countries. Always ask a parent or teacher before sharing anything online.

sec.t:
आँख के अगले पारदर्शी हिस्से, [[cornea|कॉर्निया]], में खून की नलियाँ नहीं होतीं। उसे ऑक्सीजन सीधे हवा से मिलती है, और ठीक से काम करने के लिए उसे गीला रहना पड़ता है। आँसुओं की परत बहुत पतली होती है, पर उसकी तीन तहें होती हैं। [[@gross-eye-boogers|चिपचिपी म्यूकस वाली तह]] इसे आँख से चिपकाए रखती है। बीच की पानी वाली तह हर आँख के ऊपर बनी [[gland|ग्रंथियों]] से आती है। इसमें नमक और कीटाणुओं से लड़ने वाले पदार्थ होते हैं। सबसे ऊपर की पतली तैलीय तह [[evaporation|वाष्पीकरण]], यानी पानी के भाप बनकर उड़ने, को धीमा करती है।

दो झपकियों के बीच यह परत धीरे-धीरे सूखकर टूटने लगती है। पलक झपकते ही नई परत चढ़ जाती है। इस्तेमाल हो चुके आँसू पलकों के भीतरी कोनों के नन्हे छेदों से होकर नाक में बह जाते हैं। इसीलिए रोते समय नाक भी बहने लगती है।

कुछ झपकियाँ जानबूझकर होती हैं, जैसे आँख मारना। ज़्यादातर अपने-आप होती हैं। और कुछ [[@reflexes|प्रतिवर्ती क्रियाएँ]] होती हैं, जो [[nerve|नसों]] के एक तेज़ घेरे से होकर गुज़रती हैं और दिमाग के सोचने वाले हिस्से का इंतज़ार नहीं करतीं।

पलकों के बालों या आँख की सतह को छुओ, और दोनों आँखें बंद हो जाती हैं। तेज़ धमाका या चेहरे के पास अचानक कोई हरकत भी पलक झपकवा सकती है। [[@sneezes|छींकते]] समय भी आँखें बंद हो जाती हैं, हालाँकि यह कोई पक्का नहीं जानता कि क्यों।

तुम कितनी बार पलक झपकाते हो, यह इस पर निर्भर है कि तुम कर क्या रहे हो। बातचीत में लोग बार-बार पलक झपकाते हैं। जब वे पढ़ने, गाड़ी चलाने या [[@video-games|वीडियो गेम]] में ध्यान लगाते हैं, तो पलक झपकना आधे से भी कम रह सकता है।

यही एक वजह है कि फ़ोन, टैबलेट या कंप्यूटर को देर तक घूरने के बाद आँखें सूखी, खुजलीदार या थकी लग सकती हैं। आँखों के डॉक्टर अक्सर एक आसान आदत बताते हैं: हर 20 मिनट पर, लगभग 6 मीटर दूर किसी चीज़ को 20 सेकंड तक देखो।

हर जीव हमारी तरह पलक नहीं झपकाता। साँपों की पलकें होती ही नहीं। इसकी जगह उनकी हर आँख पर एक पारदर्शी, अटल शल्क चढ़ा होता है, जो केंचुली के साथ उतर जाता है। ज़्यादातर मछलियों की भी पलकें नहीं होतीं, क्योंकि पानी उनकी आँखों को गीला रखता है।

बहुत-से पक्षियों, सरीसृपों और बिल्ली जैसे कुछ स्तनधारियों में एक तीसरी पलक होती है। यह आर-पार दिखने वाली एक झिल्ली है जो आँख पर बगल से सरककर उसे साफ़ करती और बचाती है। इंसानों की हर आँख के भीतरी कोने में बस एक नन्ही गुलाबी तह होती है। वैज्ञानिक मानते हैं कि यह हमारे बहुत पुराने [[ancestor|पूर्वजों]] की उसी तीसरी पलक की निशानी है।

बच्चे एक पहेली हैं। नवजात शिशु एक मिनट में बस एक-दो बार पलक झपकाते हैं। बचपन भर उनकी झपकियाँ धीरे-धीरे बढ़ती जाती हैं, और किशोर उम्र तक जाकर बड़ों के बराबर पहुँचती हैं।

text: तुम्हारा शरीर आधे से ज़्यादा पानी है, और उसे इस पानी का संतुलन बनाए रखना पड़ता है। जब पसीने, साँस और शौचालय के ज़रिए [[@body-no-water|पानी निकल जाता है]], तो खून थोड़ा ज़्यादा नमकीन हो जाता है और उसकी मात्रा थोड़ी घट जाती है।

दिमाग़ के निचले हिस्से में एक छोटा इलाका है, हाइपोथैलेमस। इसमें लगी ख़ास [[sensor|सेंसर]] कोशिकाएँ इस बदलाव को पकड़ लेती हैं। नमकीनपन में बस एक-दो प्रतिशत की बढ़त भी काफ़ी है। फिर दिमाग़ तुम्हें प्यास महसूस कराता है, और तुम पानी पीते हो। साथ ही वह एक [[hormone|हॉर्मोन]] छोड़ता है जो तुम्हारे [[@kidneys|गुर्दों]] से पानी बचाने को कहता है। इसीलिए पानी कम पीने पर पेशाब का रंग गहरा हो जाता है।

sec.t:
बड़ा इंसान रोज़ लगभग 2 से 3 लीटर पानी खोता है, गरम दिनों में या खेलते समय और ज़्यादा। कुछ [[@sweat|पसीने]] में जाता है, कुछ साँस में भाप बनकर (ठंडे शीशे पर साँस छोड़ो तो धुंध दिखती है), और बहुत-सा पेशाब में।

इसकी भरपाई तुम पीकर करते हो, और खाकर भी। [[@watermelon|तरबूज़]] और संतरे जैसे फल, दाल, चावल और दही, सबमें पानी होता है। शरीर खाना तोड़ते समय खुद भी थोड़ा पानी बना लेता है।

हैज़े जैसी बीमारियों से होने वाले गंभीर दस्त शरीर से पानी और नमक ख़तरनाक तेज़ी से निकाल सकते हैं, ख़ासकर छोटे बच्चों में। लंबे समय तक इसका मुख्य इलाज नस में ड्रिप लगाना था, जिसके लिए प्रशिक्षित लोग और सामान चाहिए।

1960 के दशक में ढाका और कोलकाता में काम करने वाले वैज्ञानिकों ने दिखाया कि सही मात्रा में नमक और चीनी वाला पानी हैज़े के दौरान भी आँतें सोख सकती हैं। 1971 में, बांग्लादेश मुक्ति युद्ध के दौरान, भारतीय डॉक्टर दिलीप महालनबीस सीमा के पास एक शरणार्थी शिविर चला रहे थे, जहाँ हैज़ा फैल गया। ड्रिप कम पड़ गईं, इसलिए उनकी टीम ने मरीज़ों को यही घोल पिलाया, जिसे ओआरएस कहते हैं। आम दिनों से कहीं कम लोगों की मौत हुई। आज ओआरएस दुनिया की सबसे सस्ती और सबसे अहम दवाओं में से है, और विश्व स्वास्थ्य संगठन इसकी सलाह देता है।

"रोज़ आठ गिलास" वाला पुराना नियम किसी पक्के सबूत पर नहीं टिका। ज़रूरत तुम्हारे आकार, भाग-दौड़ और मौसम के साथ बदलती है। चेन्नई की गरमी में क्रिकेट खेलते बच्चे को सर्दियों में घर के अंदर पढ़ते बच्चे से कहीं ज़्यादा पानी चाहिए।

ज़्यादातर सेहतमंद बच्चों के लिए प्यास लगने पर पीना, खाने के साथ पानी लेना, और गरमी में या खेलते समय ज़्यादा पीना ठीक काम करता है। मीठी ड्रिंक से [[@water-drink|सादा पानी]] बेहतर है। गरम दिन में चक्कर आना, बहुत थकान या सिरदर्द, पानी कम पीने के संकेत हो सकते हैं, इसलिए किसी बड़े को बताओ।

कुछ जानवर बहुत कम पानी पीकर भी जी लेते हैं। [[@camels|ऊँट]] अपने शरीर का एक चौथाई पानी खो सकते हैं और फिर कुछ ही मिनटों में 100 लीटर से ज़्यादा पी जाते हैं। उनके कूबड़ में चर्बी जमा होती है, पानी नहीं। अमेरिका के रेगिस्तानों में रहने वाले कंगारू चूहे शायद कभी पानी पीते ही नहीं, और ज़रूरत का पानी अपने खाने से ही ले लेते हैं।

text: In April 2021, a small NASA helicopter named Ingenuity lifted off from the floor of Jezero Crater on Mars. It rose three metres, hovered for about 30 seconds and landed. It was the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.

Flying on Mars is tough because the [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] is about 1% as thick as Earth's. To get lift from such thin air, Ingenuity used two sets of carbon-fibre blades, each about 1.2 metres from tip to tip, spinning in opposite directions roughly 2,400 times a minute. It weighed only about 1.8 kg, and it flew itself.

st.reveal: Mars does have air, but it is so thin that blades have very little to push against. Gravity on Mars is only about a third of Earth's, which helps a little. Ingenuity needed huge, fast-spinning blades and a body lighter than a big bag of rice.

Radio signals take between about 5 and 20 minutes to travel between Earth and Mars. Engineers sent Ingenuity a flight plan in advance, and it flew itself, using its own camera and sensors to stay on course.

sec.t:
Ingenuity travelled to Mars tucked under the belly of the [[@mars-rovers|Perseverance rover]]. They landed together on 18 February 2021. A few weeks later the [[rover|rover]] dropped it gently onto the ground and drove away so the helicopter could charge its batteries in the sunshine using a small solar panel.

The first night was a test in itself. Temperatures in Jezero can drop to around minus 90°C. Ingenuity had to use some of its battery power just to keep its electronics warm enough to survive.

sec.h: Why the blades spin so fast

sec.t:
Mars is so far away that a radio message takes between 5 and 20 minutes to arrive, depending on where the two planets are in their [[orbit|orbits]]. No pilot could steer it live. Instead, the team sent up a flight plan, and Ingenuity's onboard computer did the rest.

It used a downward-looking camera to track the ground below, plus [[sensor|sensors]] that measure tilt and speed, many of them similar to the parts in a [[@smartphones|smartphone]]. If something went wrong mid-air, it had to sort it out by itself. On its sixth flight, a glitch confused its camera timing and it wobbled wildly, but it still landed safely.

Tucked under Ingenuity's solar panel was a piece of fabric about the size of a postage stamp. It came from the Wright Flyer, the plane in which Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first powered flight at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903. NASA named Ingenuity's first airfield "Wright Brothers Field". Almost 118 years separated the two first flights.

The plan was for up to five test flights in about a month. Ingenuity kept going. It began scouting ahead for Perseverance, taking photos to help the rover's drivers choose safe routes. Over 72 flights it covered about 17 km, climbed as high as 24 metres and spent more than two hours in the air in total.

In January 2024, after its 72nd flight, photos showed that at least one [[rotor|rotor]] blade had broken. It probably struck the ground while landing on smooth sand, which gave its camera few features to track. It could no longer fly. Ingenuity stayed where it landed and, for a while, kept sending back data as a tiny weather station. NASA is building a much bigger flying machine, the Dragonfly drone, to explore Saturn's moon [[@titan|Titan]], where thick air will make flying far easier.

यूरोप में किसी को नहीं पता था कि प्रशांत कितना चौड़ा है। यह सफ़र तीन महीने से ज़्यादा चला, और उन्हें लगभग कोई ज़मीन नहीं दिखी। खाना ख़त्म हो गया। पिगाफ़ेत्ता ने लिखा कि उन्होंने कीड़े रेंगते बिस्कुट, लकड़ी का बुरादा, चूहे और समुद्री पानी में भिगोई चमड़े की पट्टियाँ खाईं।

बहुत से लोग स्कर्वी से बीमार पड़ गए, एक ऐसी बीमारी जिसमें मसूड़े सूज जाते हैं और उनसे ख़ून आता है। आज हम जानते हैं कि यह [[vitamin|विटामिन]] C की कमी से होती है, जो ताज़े फलों और सब्ज़ियों में मिलता है। मार्च 1521 में वे गुआम पहुँचे, और फिर फ़िलीपींस।

फ़िलीपींस में मैगलन ने कुछ दोस्त बनाए और स्थानीय सरदारों पर ईसाई धर्म और स्पेनी राज मानने का दबाव डाला। मक्तान द्वीप के सरदार लापुलापु ने साफ़ मना कर दिया।

27 अप्रैल 1521 को मैगलन ने थोड़े से सैनिकों के साथ हमला किया और उथले पानी में मारा गया। फ़िलीपींस में लापुलापु को ऐसे नायक के रूप में याद किया जाता है जिसने विदेशी राज का विरोध किया। मैगलन का दुभाषिया एनरीके दक्षिण-पूर्व एशिया का रहने वाला था और यूरोप से उसके साथ पश्चिम की ओर चला था। अगर वह बाद में अपने घर पहुँच गया, तो शायद धरती का चक्कर लगाने वाला पहला इंसान वही था। पर उसका क्या हुआ, कोई नहीं जानता।

सिर्फ़ विक्टोरिया ने यात्रा पूरी की, लौंग से लदा हुआ। जुलाई 1522 में जब बचे हुए लोग केप वर्डे द्वीपों पर रुके, तो पता चला कि उनकी लॉगबुक वहाँ की तारीख़ से एक दिन पीछे है।

उनका हिसाब बिल्कुल सही था। बात यह थी कि सूरज के साथ-साथ पश्चिम की ओर चलते हुए पूरी धरती घूम लेने से उन्होंने घर पर रहने वालों से एक सूर्योदय कम देखा था। आज अंतरराष्ट्रीय तिथि रेखा और [[@time-zones|टाइम ज़ोन]] ठीक इसी पहेली को सुलझाते हैं। 2017-18 में भारतीय नौसेना की छह महिला अफ़सरों ने छोटी-सी पाल वाली नाव INSV तारिणी पर दुनिया का चक्कर लगाया, और समुद्री यात्रियों की इस लंबी परंपरा को आगे बढ़ाया।

text: The Hoover Dam is a curved wall of concrete across the Colorado River, on the border between the US states of Nevada and Arizona. It is 221 metres tall, about the height of a 60-storey building, and around 200 metres thick at the bottom. That's nearly the length of two football fields laid end to end.

It holds back Lake Mead, one of the largest [[reservoir|reservoirs]] in the United States. Water rushing through its [[turbine|turbines]] makes electricity for over a million people, and the lake supplies water to farms and cities in the dry southwest.

No bodies are in the dam. The concrete was poured in small blocks, a little at a time, and the people who died were recovered. The official count of deaths during construction is 96.

sec.t:
The Colorado River used to flood in spring and nearly dry up in late summer. Farmers downstream in California could lose their crops either way. A dam could store the floodwater and let it out slowly through the year, while making power.

Work began in 1931, during the [[@great-depression|Great Depression]], when millions of Americans had lost their jobs. Thousands of men came to the hot, empty desert looking for work. At the peak, more than 5,000 people were working on the dam at once.

The dam was not poured as one giant slab. It was built from hundreds of separate column-shaped blocks, each a metre or two high at a time. That was because [[@cement-concrete|concrete]] gives off heat as it hardens. Poured all at once, engineers worked out, it would have taken more than a hundred years to cool and would have cracked.

So workers laid steel pipes through each block and pumped icy water through them. A plant nearby made ice for the job. About 2.5 million cubic metres of concrete went into the dam. It was finished in 1936, two years ahead of schedule.

Water from the lake drops through giant pipes and spins 17 turbines at the foot of the dam, the same idea that drives [[@dams-power|hydroelectric dams]] everywhere. Together they can produce about 2,000 megawatts of electricity, and no fuel has to be burned to make it. Much of it goes to Nevada, Arizona and California, including the lights of [[@las-vegas|Las Vegas]], about 50 kilometres away.

The dam sits right on a state line, and for half the year Nevada and Arizona keep different clocks. Arizona doesn't change its clocks in summer, while Nevada does. So in summer, two clocks on the dam's towers show different times, a quirk of [[@time-zones|time zones]].

Lake Mead depends on snow melting in the Rocky Mountains. After many dry years, the water dropped to its lowest level ever recorded in July 2022, when the lake was only about a quarter full. Old boats and buildings that had been underwater for decades appeared on the shore.

[[@droughts|Droughts]] and growing cities mean the seven states that share the Colorado River must agree on how much water each can take, and those talks are often tough. India has its own giant dams too. The Bhakra Dam on the Sutlej, finished in 1963, is about as tall as Hoover, and the Tehri Dam in Uttarakhand is taller still.

text: The Mississippi is the main river of the United States. It begins as a small stream flowing out of Lake Itasca in Minnesota and runs about 3,700 kilometres south to the Gulf of Mexico. Along the way, big rivers such as the Missouri and the Ohio pour into it.

Its basin, the whole area whose rain ends up in the river, covers about 40 percent of the 48 joined-up states. That makes it the drain for the American heartland, the flat farmland where much of the country's maize and soybeans grow. For thousands of years it has been a highway for boats, a source of food and a dividing line between east and west. It has also flooded towns and farms again and again.

sec.h: From a trickle to a giant
sec.t:
At Lake Itasca, the young river is so shallow and narrow that visitors hop across it on stepping stones. By the time it reaches St Louis, after the Missouri joins it, it carries a vast load of mud from the Great Plains. The Missouri brings so much of it that people nicknamed that river the "Big Muddy".

Near its mouth, below [[@new-orleans|New Orleans]], the river slows and drops that mud. Over thousands of years it has built a huge [[@deltas|delta]], pushing new land into the sea in a shape that looks like a bird's foot from above.

Samuel Clemens grew up in Hannibal, Missouri, a town on the riverbank, in the 1840s. As a young man he trained as a steamboat pilot, which meant memorising every bend, sandbar and snag over more than a thousand kilometres of water.

When he became a writer he called himself [[@mark-twain|Mark Twain]], after a cry used by boatmen measuring the depth. His books *The Adventures of Tom Sawyer* and *Adventures of Huckleberry Finn* are full of the river: rafts, islands, storms and the life of river towns. In *Life on the Mississippi*, he wrote about how the river kept changing its course.

sec.h: Floods and a river that wants to move
sec.t:
The Mississippi has always flooded. In 1927, after months of heavy rain, it burst through its banks in many places and covered about 70,000 square kilometres, roughly the size of Assam. Hundreds of thousands of people had to leave their homes.

After that, engineers built thousands of kilometres of levees, high earth banks along the river. They also built a set of gates in Louisiana called the Old River Control Structure. Left alone, the Mississippi would probably have switched much of its flow into a shorter, steeper channel, the Atchafalaya River, decades ago. The gates hold it in place, because ports and cities depend on the river staying where it is.

text: The Qutub Minar is a tall stone tower in the south of [[@delhi|Delhi]]. It is about 73 metres high, roughly a 24-storey building, and narrows from about 14 metres wide at the bottom to under 3 metres at the top. It is made of red and buff sandstone, with white marble in its upper storeys.

Work on it began in the 1190s, under Qutb ud-din Aibak, the first ruler of what became the [[@delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]]. A minaret, or [[minaret|minar]], is a tower beside a mosque from which the call to prayer can be given. This one was also a victory tower, built to announce that a new power had arrived in north India.

st.prompt: What protects Delhi's 1,600-year-old Iron Pillar from rusting away?

options.t: A thin, tough layer that formed on its surface, helped by phosphorus in the iron
A secret paint that ancient workers brushed on every year
Delhi's air is too dry for iron to rust

st.reveal: The pillar's iron has a lot of phosphorus and very little sulphur. Over time, this helped a thin protective film form on the surface, which slows rusting to a crawl. Scientists at IIT Kanpur studied the pillar in detail to work this out.

src: Archaeological Survey of India, Qutb Minar and its Monuments.
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Qutb Minar and its Monuments, Delhi.
n.certNote: Historians agree on who began and finished the tower, but they disagree on its name. Some say it is named after Qutb ud-din Aibak, who started it, and others after the Sufi saint Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki.

d.try: Estimate a tall building's height without climbing it. Count its storeys and multiply by about 3 metres per storey. Then work out how many of those buildings, stacked up, would match the Qutub Minar's 73 metres.
myth: Delhi's Iron Pillar never rusts at all.
It does rust, but extremely slowly. A thin protective layer on its surface keeps the rusting from eating deep into the metal, so after 1,600 years it is still standing strong.
facts: in the 1190s, by Qutb ud-din Aibak
about 7 m tall and about 1,600 years old

sec.t:
Aibak lived to see only the first storey finished. His successor, Iltutmish, added three more. In 1368, lightning struck the top and damaged it. The ruler Firoz Shah Tughlaq repaired it, rebuilding the top floor and adding a fifth storey faced with white marble.

You can still see the change if you look up. The lower storeys are deep red and buff, while the top ones are paler. Each storey is ringed by a balcony held up on carved stone brackets, and the outer walls swirl with fluted ribs, some rounded and some sharp-edged.

In the courtyard stands the Iron Pillar, about 7 metres tall. An inscription in Sanskrit suggests it was made around 1,600 years ago, in the time of the [[@gupta-golden-age|Gupta]] kings, probably to honour the god Vishnu. It was moved to Delhi centuries later.

Most iron left outdoors flakes into [[@rust|rust]] within years. This pillar has survived about 16 centuries with only a thin coat. Metal scientists, including R. Balasubramaniam of IIT Kanpur, found that its iron is rich in phosphorus. This helped a thin, tight protective layer form on its surface, slowing rusting almost to a stop. It also shows how skilled Indian ironworkers were.

sec.h: Stairs, storms and a dome on the lawn
sec.t:
Inside the tower, a spiral staircase of 379 steps climbs to the top. Visitors once climbed it, but in 1981 a crowd accident on the stairs killed dozens of people, many of them schoolchildren. The tower has been closed inside ever since.

The Qutub Minar has survived [[@lightning|lightning]] and earthquakes. After an earthquake in 1803 damaged the top, a British officer, Major Robert Smith, added a small domed pavilion as a new crown in 1828. People thought it looked out of place, and it was taken down about 20 years later. It now sits on the lawn nearby, sometimes called "Smith's Folly".

Near the Qutub Minar stands a wide, stumpy ring of rubble about 25 metres high. This is the Alai Minar. In the early 1300s, Sultan Alauddin Khalji began it, planning a tower twice as big as the Qutub Minar. He died in 1316 and nobody finished it.

Together, these buildings form the Qutb complex, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993. Like the [[@red-fort|Red Fort]], it draws visitors from across India and the world, and the sight of the tower against the evening sky has hardly changed in more than 600 years.

text: Route 66 is a highway in the United States that opened in 1926. It ran about 3,940 kilometres (2,448 miles) from [[@chicago|Chicago]] in the Midwest to Santa Monica on the Pacific coast, passing through eight states. That is a little more than the distance from Srinagar to Kanyakumari.

For decades it was the main road west. Farm families escaping hard times drove it, then holidaymakers in shiny new cars. Diners, motels and petrol stations with glowing signs sprang up beside it. When faster motorways replaced it, the old road became something new: a symbol of travel and freedom. Its 100th birthday falls on 11 November 2026.

st.prompt: Route 66 was nearly given a different number. Which one did its planners first want?

Route 99

st.reveal: Officials from Oklahoma and Missouri wanted the road to be US 60. Kentucky also claimed that number, and after months of argument the planners settled on 66. It turned out to be a catchy choice.

src: National Park Service, Route 66 Corridor Preservation Program.
Britannica, Route 66.
Steinbeck J. (1939) The Grapes of Wrath.

myth: Route 66 doesn't exist any more.

It was taken off the official US highway list in 1985, but much of the old road is still there. Long stretches are signed as "Historic Route 66", and you can still drive most of the way from Chicago to the Pacific.
facts: Chicago, Illinois, to Santa Monica, California
Illinois, Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, California
the Mother Road, from John Steinbeck's 1939 novel
Removed from the US highway system

sec.t:
In the early 1900s, most American roads were dirt tracks that turned to mud in the rain. As [[@cars-history|cars]] became cheaper, people demanded better ones. In 1926, the government created a national system of numbered highways.

A businessman from Oklahoma, Cyrus Avery, pushed hard for one road to link Chicago with Los Angeles. Unlike older roads that ran straight east to west, it curved south-west through small towns, giving farmers a way to get crops to market. Much of it was still gravel or dirt at first. It was paved from end to end by 1938.

After the Second World War, Americans had more money and more cars. Families took road trips on Route 66 for fun. A 1946 song told listeners to "get your kicks on Route 66", and it became a hit.

Businesses competed for travellers' attention. There were motels shaped like wigwams, giant concrete dinosaurs and towering neon signs. Diners served burgers and milkshakes to people who had driven all day across the desert. One famous detour leads to the [[@grand-canyon|Grand Canyon]], about an hour's drive north of the road in Arizona.

In 1956, the US began building the interstate highways: wide, fast motorways that skip around towns instead of going through them. Bit by bit, new interstates replaced Route 66. The last town on the old road, Williams in Arizona, was bypassed in 1984. The next year, Route 66 was removed from the official list.

Many towns that had lived off passing travellers faded. Motels closed and signs went dark. It's a pattern seen in many countries: when a new highway or railway goes elsewhere, the towns on the old route can lose their customers almost overnight.

Fans of the old road started campaigning to save it. States put up brown "Historic Route 66" signs, and old motels and diners were restored. Visitors from Europe, Japan and India now rent cars to drive it.

The 2006 [[@pixar|Pixar]] film *Cars* is set in Radiator Springs, an imaginary town on a forgotten stretch of the road. Its makers drove Route 66 to research it, and many details come from real places along the way. Engineers who studied how [[@roads-built|roads are built]] in 1926 would barely recognise today's interstates. The Mother Road still runs past the same small towns.

text: The Booker Prize is one of the most famous awards for a novel written in English. It began in 1969, and the winner now gets £50,000. Each year a panel of five judges reads more than a hundred and fifty novels. They pick a longlist of about 13, cut it to a shortlist of six, and name one winner in the autumn.
For a writer, the money is the small part. A Booker winner gets reviews, translations and huge sales. Some winning books end up on school reading lists around the world.

The judges are usually a mix of novelists, critics, academics and sometimes an actor or musician. They meet many times over the summer. Each judge must read every book submitted, which can mean three or four novels a week for months.

It started as a prize for writers from the UK, Ireland and the Commonwealth, which included India. Since 2014 any novel written in English can win, if it is published in the UK or Ireland.

sec.h: A prize named after a food company
sec.t:
The name comes from Booker McConnell, a British company that traded in sugar and food. It paid for the prize at the start. From 2002 to 2019 an investment firm called the Man Group sponsored it, so it was called the Man Booker. Now it is simply the Booker again.

For many years only writers from the UK, Ireland and the Commonwealth could enter. In 2014 the rules opened up to any novel in English published in Britain or Ireland. Two years later, Paul Beatty became the first American to win, for *The Sellout*. Some British writers worried that big American publishers would crowd out everyone else. Others said a prize for English writing should welcome English from anywhere.

A sister award, the International Booker Prize, is given to a book translated into English. The prize money is shared equally between the author and the translator, which shows how much skill [[@translation|translation]] takes.

In 2022 Geetanjali Shree's Hindi novel *Ret Samadhi* won as *Tomb of Sand*, translated by the American Daisy Rockwell. In 2025 the Kannada writer Banu Mushtaq won for *Heart Lamp*, a collection of short stories translated by Deepa Bhasthi. It was the first story collection to win.

Book prizes always cause arguments, and the Booker enjoys them. Readers grumble that a favourite was left out. In 2019 the judges refused to choose between two books and split the prize between Margaret Atwood and Bernardine Evaristo, even though the rules said they should not.

A few writers have won twice, including Hilary Mantel, J. M. Coetzee and Peter Carey. Nobody has won three times yet. Mantel's two winners were both about Thomas Cromwell, an adviser to King Henry VIII, which made her the first to win with a book and its sequel. The judges change every year, so nobody can be sure what the next panel will love. That uncertainty is part of the fun of watching from [[@london|London]] or from Lucknow.

text: Narnia is a magical land in a series of seven children's books by C. S. Lewis, called *The Chronicles of Narnia*, published between 1950 and 1956. It is a world of talking animals, fauns, giants, dwarfs and witches, ruled over by a great lion named Aslan, whose name is simply the Turkish word for lion.

In each book, children from our world find their way into Narnia, most famously through the back of a wardrobe. They have adventures, fight evil and grow braver, then return home, often finding that almost no time has passed. The books have sold more than 100 million copies and been turned into radio plays, TV series and films. For many readers, Narnia is the first [[@fantasy-books|fantasy world]] they ever fall in love with.

st.reveal: Mr Tumnus explains that the Witch has made it "always winter and never Christmas". When Aslan returns, the snow begins to melt and Father Christmas finally arrives, a sign that the spell is breaking.
