The wardrobe is used in one book. In others, children get in through magic rings, a painting of a ship, a railway station platform, and a door in a school wall.
facts: C. S. Lewis (1898–1963), born in Belfast
The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, 1950

sec.t:
Clive Staples Lewis was born in 1898 in Belfast, in what is now Northern Ireland, part of the [[@uk-countries|UK]]. His family called him Jack. As a boy he and his brother invented an imaginary country of talking animals, which they wrote about and drew.

Lewis later wrote that Narnia started with a picture he had carried in his head since he was about 16: a faun carrying an umbrella and parcels through a snowy wood. Many years later, when he was around fifty, he decided to write a story around it. That faun became Mr Tumnus, the first creature Lucy meets in Narnia.

Narnia mixes creatures from many traditions. Fauns, centaurs and the god Bacchus come from [[@greek-myths|Greek and Roman myths]]. Dwarfs and giants come from northern European tales. Father Christmas appears in the first book.

Lewis's friend J.R.R. Tolkien did not like this mix. He thought a made-up world should hang together more carefully. Lewis didn't mind.

Lewis was a Christian, and many readers see Aslan as a picture of Jesus, especially when he gives his life for Edmund and then returns. Lewis said he did not intend a simple allegory, where each character stands for something else. He described it as imagining what Christ might be like in a world like Narnia. Some later writers, such as Philip Pullman, have criticised the books for their religious message and for how they treat Susan at the end of the series.

The books were published in one order and happen in another. *The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe* came out first, but *The Magician's Nephew*, published in 1955, tells how Narnia was created, so it comes first in Narnia's own history.

Many modern editions number the books in story order. Others argue that new readers should meet Narnia through the wardrobe, as the first readers did. In a 1957 letter to a young American fan, Lewis said he thought story order was probably fine, but that it didn't much matter. Readers have been arguing about it ever since.

text: A pun is a joke that plays with a word that has two meanings, or two words that sound alike. "I used to be a banker, but I lost interest." The sentence makes sense one way, then suddenly makes sense another way too.

Scientists think puns are funny because of that sudden switch. Your brain reads the sentence, expects one meaning, hits a surprise, and then solves the puzzle. That quick "aha" can feel good, and it can make you [[@laughter|laugh]].
Puns also make people groan. That groan is part of the game. It says: "I see what you did there, and I wish I didn't."

st.prompt: In China, many families eat fish at New Year. Why?

options.t: The word for fish sounds like the word for "plenty"
Fish are the cheapest food in winter

st.reveal: In Mandarin, yu (fish) sounds like the word for surplus or abundance. Eating fish is a spoken wish for plenty in the year ahead, a pun you can eat.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Pun.

Sheldon Pollock (2003), Literary Cultures in History, University of California Press.
n.certNote: How puns work, using double meanings, is well understood. Why our brains enjoy them, and why they make some people groan, is still studied, and scientists have several competing ideas.

d.try: Pick a word with two meanings, like "bat", "bark" or "light". Write one sentence where both meanings could work at once. Try it on someone and watch their face for the half-second pause before they get it, then groan or laugh.
myth: Great writers avoid puns because they are a low, lazy kind of joke.
Some of the greatest writers in history loved puns. Shakespeare packed his plays with them, and Sanskrit poets turned double meanings into a high art called shlesha.

sec.t:
[[@shakespeare|Shakespeare]] loved puns. By some counts there are more than 3,000 in his plays. In Romeo and Juliet, Mercutio is fatally wounded in a sword fight. Even then he jokes: "Ask for me tomorrow, and you shall find me a grave man." He means serious, and he means a man in his grave.

People in Shakespeare's time found puns clever and stylish. Later, some critics in the 1700s and 1800s looked down on them as cheap. Today, newspaper headlines, adverts and children's books use them everywhere.

Sanskrit poets took puns further than almost anyone. They called the art shlesha, meaning "embrace", because two meanings hold each other in one line. A single verse might describe a king and the Moon at the same time, with every word fitting both.

Around 900 years ago, a poet called Kaviraja wrote the Raghavapandaviya. Read one way, each verse tells part of the Ramayana. Read another way, the very same words tell the Mahabharata. Writing it meant choosing every word in the language of [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] to carry two jobs.

Indian folk tales are full of wordplay too. Clever heroes like [[@tenali-raman|Tenali Raman]] and Birbal often win by twisting the meaning of a king's command.

In Chinese, many words sound alike, so puns are part of everyday life and art. The word for fish, yu, sounds like the word for abundance. That is why fish is served at Lunar New Year. The word for bat sounds like the word for good fortune, so bats appear on old Chinese plates and silk as lucky symbols.

Because [[@chinese-characters|Chinese characters]] show meaning as well as sound, a pun can be written with one character but heard as another. Some New Year decorations play on this, hanging a sign for "good fortune" upside down, because "upside down" sounds like "arrived".

Since 1978, Austin, Texas, has hosted the O. Henry Pun-Off World Championships. Contestants stand on stage and fire puns at each other on a set topic, sometimes for minutes without stopping. The audience groans loudest at the best ones.

Puns are a little like riddles. Both hide a second meaning in plain sight and reward the listener who finds it. And the strangest part? Some of the world's oldest [[@riddles|riddles]], from ancient Greece to India, work exactly the same way.
